title: Hold, and Don't Look Down
blurb: Dagny has to win on nothing but trust and a hair's turn, because one paid pound tips her Heavy, and Pru has been keeping a secret since the night it all began.

blocks.text: A week I had carried it knowing, and I still hadn't cut it open.

I stood on the Lip at Coldhithe with my left hand in my father's coat pocket and the two fingers that don't close lying on the square of stitching through the lining, and I looked down into a shaft that was built wrong. Two of its ledges sat one above the other on the same wall, six metres apart. When the walls fell our way, both of them would be ours.
Hal came and stood beside me and looked down at them too.
"Aye," he said. "Steady."
He said it as if he already knew what I was going to ask him.

I had felt the square every night that week, lying flat on the boards at home with the coat over me. Paper, folded small, with a stiff edge at one corner. On the Tuesday I put the kitchen knife's point to the first stitch, and then I put the knife back in the drawer. My father had written down what Osk weighed when he lifted him out of the Settle. Whatever else he had written, I could not carry it into this shaft as well. I knew my load to the pound. I did not know what the paper weighed.

He had sewn it where his own hip would have been, flat, so a man could lean on a lift lever all day and never feel it. He hadn't sewn it for me. But Sibbald Teague had told me that my father always knew what a cage weighed, and every night I had lain with my hand over the square and wondered how Teague knew it, and who else did.
Rafe had said he would come on the coal cart after us, in time for the bell. He wasn't on the Lip. I looked for him twice more, and then I made myself stop.
The Lip at Coldhithe is reached by twenty-two iron steps from the yard. I had to stop on the eleventh with both hands on the rail and wait for my knees.
The Weighman read the scale and wrote. "Four stone and a pound over, Miss Quillon." His pencil stopped at the small mark in the margin by my name, the way it had the week before, and went on.

Four stone and a pound in the book. Five stone and thirteen pounds in my bones, all of it lean, the Tallymen's carry long drained out of me on the boards. Six stone is Heavy. Six stone is where a ladder becomes a wall. An ounce an hour, near enough, so the lean alone would take me over by tomorrow. In the shaft it would be quicker. The Cob held in any set that wasn't true down cost seven pounds a minute. A man cost fourteen. One pound was eight counts of Cob, four counts of man.
So I could not pay for anything. Whatever we won today we would win on true down and on nulls, which cost nothing, or we would not win.

The Ropers had the Twin wall for the first Drop, by the Weighman's coin. Their two Anchors took L3 and L4, one over the other, and at the bell they set both zones the same way, straight across at our wall. Where the two zones overlapped, the sets added. Two plumb, sideways. The Cob came down into it and went across the shaft as if it had been thrown, struck our wall below Hal's ledge and slid down it into our well at forty counts.
I was on L5. I could have turned my set and pushed it back across. I held true down and let it go past me, and it was the hardest thing my hand had done all season.
Nil to three.
At the Hoist the walls swapped, and the Twin wall was ours.
I went to Hal on the planks. He had his hand flat on his strapped side, and when he saw me he took it away, and then he put it back. That was new.

"L3 straight up," I said. "Exactly up. I hold L4 at true down under you. Where the zones overlap, your up and my down cancel, and nothing in that Lap falls. Their Anchors can't touch it. Both its Pins are ours."
"I can't feel straight up to a degree," Hal said. "Nobody can."

"I can see it. There's a rope tail off L3 that hangs down through the Lap. When you're off, it leans. I'll call you a hair at a time and you turn on my voice. You don't look down to check. If you look down you lean out, and your hand goes with you."
He said nothing for a moment. Before the Coopers he had stood on our own Lip with his hand pressed to his side and called me a liability, and I had believed him.
"Aye," he said.

It went into my chest and sat there, warm. He was going to hold whatever I told him and not look, and I was going to tell him the truth to the degree, and I had never in my life been trusted like that.
Osk, in his chair at the rail, lifted one finger. "One: Hal holds. Two: she counts. Three: nobody goes into her zone. Not you, Dunnet. Not the Cob."
Dunnet laughed, the big laugh, too loud for the size of the Lip. "Their Dropper's got arms like a winch, Counts. He won't come near you. He'll want to be up with Hal, where it's lively."
Lisbet lowered me to L4 in the sling. Hal went to L3, six metres over my head, on the same wall.
"Bell," Pru called from the platform. "Cob's live. Evens, evens."
Hal turned L3 straight up and stood. I held L4 at true down. It cost me nothing, and I counted the nothing, because it was the only number all day I could afford.
The rope tail off L3 hung down past him into the Lap. It leaned toward the far wall.
"Toward us," I called. "A hair."
It leaned less.
"Hair."
It stopped leaning. It didn't fall and it didn't rise. It hung there in the lamplight and did nothing at all.
"Hold," I said.
Hal hummed his one note, low, and did not look down.

The Cob came down through their L2 zone, steered at our wall, dropped into Hal's set above the Lap and stopped as if it had hit a roof, and their L2 set pressed it against our wall. Their Dropper went up a rope for it. So did Dunnet, and when two men want one Cob on one rope the heavier man keeps it. He tucked it under his arm and came down hand under hand toward the Lap, against Hal's set, which pushed him up the whole way.

Hal paid for every count of it. A head and a half for Dunnet, half a head for the Cob, at one plumb straight up: two stone a minute, Hal's alone. I counted it for him because he couldn't count and hold. Ten counts, a third of a stone. Their Dropper stayed in Hal's zone on purpose, another stone a minute on top. Fourteen counts. Eighteen. Hal hummed.
At twenty counts Dunnet let go of the rope and came into the Lap, and stopped.

He didn't fall. He laid himself out flat along the null, so that no part of him stuck up into Hal's zone or down into mine, with the Cob against his chest, and he hung over the middle of Coldhithe's shaft like a man lying on a bench, and it cost nobody anything.
Their Anchors could not reach him. Their L2 zone ended metres above the Lap, and their L5 zone began below my ledge. Every Lap I had played all season had been half theirs. This one wasn't.
"Far wall's bare," Pru shouted. "Seven-to-two you're over, Dunnet. Go on."

He put his boots against our wall and pushed. He drifted across the shaft in a straight line, slow, with no field anywhere to bend him, and nobody could set a thing in his way. At the far wall he caught a fixed rope off their L2 and swung down it, out of the Lap and into my zone.

Into true down. Free. He went down the rope fast, twelve metres across the shaft from me. Below my ledge was their L5 zone, and where it met mine was a Lap with my true down in it, and whatever their L5 Anchor did in there, I would pay half of.
So I let go. Breathe in. Feel the Pin go quiet. Breath and hand together, little finger last. Three counts. My hand came off the iron, and the Lap below me was hers alone.

She turned it straight up at Dunnet. He was on a rope, so it was no foul. He hung there with the Cob under his arm and climbed down against her set the way you'd climb up, and every count of him was hers: two heads, two stone a minute. She lasted twenty-six counts and let go. Dunnet slid the rest of the way into the Throat, where nothing can be set, and put the Cob into their well with his hand like a man posting a letter.
Three all.
Level, so the Weighman's coin decided the walls for the last Drop, and Pru called it right. We kept the Twin wall.

They knew the shape now. Their Dropper went into Hal's zone at the bell and hung there on a rope to bleed him, a stone a minute. Every time the rope tail leaned I called a hair and Hal turned a hair without looking, and every time it hung still I said "Hold," and he hummed. I counted his carry out loud so he would know someone was counting it: a third of a stone, a half, three quarters. At a stone and a half Dunnet was across. Their L5 Anchor didn't turn against him this time. She had done the sum too.
Six to three.
At the scale my number hadn't moved a pound. Every ounce of that match had been Hal's, and I told him so, on the planks, plainly.
"Aye," he said, and went down the iron steps one at a time, with his hand on his side.
Five crowns each. Pru said second in the table was ours if the Saltpan result went the right way, and we would know by morning. "Evens," she said, and didn't smile.
Rafe wasn't on the Lip. I looked along the rail, and down into the yard, and along the rail again. He missed the cart, I told myself, and the telling didn't go down.
We went home with Osk's chair roped in the back of the cart and me on the tailboard, because Lisbet wouldn't let me walk two miles of it.
Halfway, on the long stretch past the Coldhithe tips, Pru came up beside the tailboard and walked there for a quarter of a mile without a word.
"I wrote Rafe's slip," she said.
The cart went on. Nobody else spoke.

"Until the night of the Coopers I kept Mr Teague's book," Pru said. Flat, the way she always talked off the shaft. "On the side. You all knew I'd been a bookie. You didn't know I still was, or whose. Two days before the Coopers he told me to take your brother's bet if he came in, and he told me the price. Fours. The gate board had us at two-to-one all week, and he wanted fours on that slip. I wrote it. Rafe signed it and went off pleased with himself."
My throat closed. My right hand had found the edge of the tailboard and was holding it hard enough to hurt.

"An hour before the bell Wat Ellery walked out in his new boots, and I understood the order," Pru said. "If you played, you played unregistered. The ringer clause on the back of the slip voids the match. Stakes held by the book. Mr Teague never wanted that bet to pay. He wanted it to void. I said nothing. I called the match. That night I gave him back his book and I never took another slip. And I never told you, or Rafe."
"I'm angry with you," I said. It came out rough. "I'm so angry with you I can't feel my hand."
"I know."

And under the anger, where she couldn't see it, was a coal chit with my handwriting on it: the odds I had worked for the Ninepins three weeks before the Coopers and left where Rafe would find them. I was angry with Pru, and I had no right to be as angry as I was, and I was anyway.
"He had us both, Counts," Dunnet said quietly, from the other side of the cart. "His book. Same as me."
Lisbet said, "Right," and nothing else.
"You tell Rafe," I said to Pru. "Yourself. Tonight."
"Tonight." She walked on beside me. "I know every Anchor in the Shaft League by how they turn. I'll write it down for you. Every one of them, priced."
"Write it," I said. "I'm still angry."
She had kept a thing from us for seven weeks, and I could see what the keeping had cost her. I was keeping one too.

"I've something to tell you," I said, louder, so the ones walking ahead would hear. My throat had shut on it and I made it open. "I'm leaning. Since the Coopers. I let go wrong the first match, before anyone taught me the Release. Osk knows. Nobody else."
The cart wheels went on. Osk, in his chair in the back, didn't turn his head.

"It puts a stone a week on me, and nothing outside the Settle takes it off. I'm five stone thirteen in my bones today. By tomorrow I'll be past six, and that's Heavy. The steps up the Lip stopped me halfway this morning. The book shows four, because I registered heavy and nobody checked. The Step is a week off, and I don't know yet how I play it."
Dunnet opened his mouth, and I saw the joke in it, and he shut it again.
Hal walked on beside the wheel for a while. "Aye," he said.
That was all he said, and it was enough. It meant he had heard the number, and he would hold whatever I asked him to hold next Monday, and he would not look down to check.
"Then I rope you," Lisbet said. "Ledge to Pin. You move when I say move."
Nobody asked me if I was all right. I loved them for it, every one of them, and I held on to the tailboard and let them walk me home.
Rafe wasn't home either.
The kitchen was dark and the fire was out. There was a note on the table, and I knew his hand from the door. I put my five crowns down beside it, against the hundred and four, before I read it.

Dags. Gone to Mr Teague to sign onto the House deep-lift crew in Shaft Four. Ten years, and he says that clears all of it, the hundred and four and everything that's coming. You won't have to carry me any more, will you? R.

A House cage, on a House cable, and my brother in it, sixteen years old, for ten years, to pay for a bet whose odds I had worked out for him on a coal chit and left where he would see them. The cold came into my hands first and then into my throat, and my knees went, and I sat down on the kitchen floor with the note in my right hand, while the door key on its nail tilted a finger's width toward me the way it had every morning since the Coopers, and I said to my father the only thing I had left to say.
"Man in the cage, Da. Hold the brake."
